items.title: Live: ASX to open higher after US tariff announcement
paras: The Australian Securities Exchange, or ASX, began trading higher this morning after shares in the United States fell overnight. That drop followed President Donald Trump’s announcement of new tariffs on goods from more than a dozen trade partners.

Investors reacted because tariffs threaten export earnings for Australian firms that rely on U.S. markets. The market muted the U.S. sell‑off, indicating Australian investors remain confident in stronger domestic support. This trend shows that global trade policy uncertainties are still tempered by local economic fundamentals.
Watch how the ASX performs as the U.S. markets settle.

items.title: US stocks tumble as AI rout and Trump tariffs rattle markets
paras: Fears are mounting over AI returns and new tariffs on US trading partners. ( Reuters: Brendan McDermid )
US stocks linked to AI continued to see share prices fall amid a sell-off in early trading on Wednesday.
Wall Street has also been rattled by new tariffs on US trading partners.
The Nasdaq plunged by about four per cent in early trading on Wednesday amid mounting doubt over whether the debt-fuelled AI boom can deliver sufficient returns.
Fear of increased regulatory scrutiny of the sector following the Democratic sweep in the midterm elections has added to the pressure during a turbulent month for Wall Street.
"The fundamental support for a year-end rally simply isn't there," SWBC chief investment officer Chris Brigati said in a note.

"The AI-inspired rally continues to run out of steam, and without evidence that massive capex spending will deliver the profit and revenue goals the market expects, there is little incentive for a rebound."

Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO provided a temporary reprieve at the start of the week, but broader concerns lingered and the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the S&P 500 remained on track for their worst November since 2008.
Chip makers led the declines, with Nvidia falling 8.7 per cent and the broader Philadelphia Semiconductor Index losing 7.3 per cent.
Among other megacaps, Alphabet fell 5 per cent, Amazon shed 5.4 per cent, and Microsoft and Apple were down 3 per cent and 1.7 per cent, respectively.
Anthropic slipped 2.1 per cent, closing on Tuesday at US$81.90, below its US$83 IPO price after a blockbuster market debut last week.
The Nasdaq 100 briefly fell 20 per cent from its record closing high, flirting with bear market territory.
Meanwhile, the US proposed new tariffs on 14 major trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions.

China will face the highest tariff rates, with the proposed 20 per cent excess-capacity levies being in addition to the roughly 25 per cent duties imposed during US President Donald Trump's first term.

The extra tariffs could cloud the outlook for investors grappling with the prospect of interest rates staying higher for longer, as inflation has accelerated and oil prices have seen a sustained rise tied to the US-Iran war.
Tariff concerns were overshadowing economic data, B. Riley Wealth chief market strategist Art Hogan said.

The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027.

At 11:28 am, US time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 602.93 points, or 1.21 per cent, to 49,415.77, the S&P 500 lost 181.04 points, or 2.51 per cent, to 7,020.05, and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 899.93 points, or 3.79 per cent per cent to 22,833.60.
The S&P 500 technology sector led the losses with a 5.2 per cent fall. Most other sectors on the benchmark were also trading in negative territory.
In other stocks, Dell Technologies fell 7 per cent even after raising its annual revenue and profit forecasts.
Rival PC maker HP gained 11.7 per cent after reporting fourth-quarter revenue and profit above analysts' estimates.
US markets will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, local time, and operate a shortened session on Friday.
Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.05-to-1 ratio on the NYSE and by a 2.97-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq.
The S&P 500 posted 8 new 52-week highs and 11 new lows, while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 17 new highs and 424 new lows.

items.title: Tom Tate's lucrative bowls-land deal with major Australian developer revealed
paras: Tom Tate's company secured a final property on a bowls site even though he was not the proposed buyer. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale )
Gold Coast Mayor Tom Tate was able to take over from colossal Australian developer Meriton the private purchase of a long-desired slice of prime real estate, the ABC can reveal.

That transfer allowed Mr Tate to purchase a sliver of land to weld with three existing blocks his private entities already co-owned in Surfers Paradise. The four-term politician and partners then flipped those combined properties in a $33 million site deal.

The mayor and Meriton, which has multiple Gold Coast projects, declined to answer questions including what the politician's private company paid for the development company's option rights for the land.
"The matters raised relate to private commercial matters," the mayor's office told the ABC.
Mr Tate's property acquisition last year had previously created controversy.
But Meriton's involvement has not previously been reported, while the seller says he had not planned on the mayor being the acquirer.
About 600 metres from golden beaches and five minutes' walk from Cavill Avenue's glitz, the former bowls club land is now prime real estate in Australia's sixth-biggest city.
Mr Tate, 67, promotes the city as "open for business" and has a headline-grabbing profile, even last month winning a Masters Pan Pacific powerlifting title.
He has retained development interests, with the mayor's property business touting plans 13 years ago for a 389-unit residential tower and 216-apartment hotel on that site.
Court and land records show a property group associated with Mr Tate, who entered politics in 2012, acquired two blocks there in 2007 for $770,000, and another for almost $2.3 million in 2016.
But council owned a final fourth block needed to complete a development site.
In 2022, that fourth block went up for public tender, and a Turner Family Properties subsidiary acquired it for $1.785 million.
Tom Tate entities co-owned properties in A since 2007, but only secured the final B property in 2025. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins/Dominic Cansdale )

The company's Peter Turner appeared on the newly bought land in a social media post. "With over 90m frontage to the Gold Coast Highway, and unlimited height zoning, we are excited," the company posted.
The family business had floated building a medical centre, although questions remained about property access that Mr Turner maintained he could secure.
In early 2025, real estate agent Roland Evans approached. He told the ABC that developer Meriton had considered acquiring the Turner land and the other three blocks linked to Mr Tate.
Documents seen by the ABC show an initial offer stated Meriton or a fully owned subsidiary acting as a nominee would acquire that Turner family company-owned land.

Around April 2025, the Turner subsidiary and a Meriton subsidiary signed an option contract to buy the land for $3.8 million excluding GST. But contract conditions included that Meriton subsidiary could nominate someone else to acquire the land.
Mr Evans, who a year later attended a controversial Mar-a-Lago dinner involving Mr Tate and US president Donald Trump, said this was a normal contract condition of which the seller was aware.
Within months, Meriton transferred its purchasing right to the company Crestden, of which Mr Tate is director and owns half the shares.

Meriton told the ABC it conducted due diligence before ultimately deciding against acquiring "the site for commercial reasons". Meriton would "not comment on the commercial terms of individual transactions".

Property records show Meriton's subsidiary temporarily took a caveat against that Turner family block during the option period but did not secure one against the other three blocks linked to Mr Tate's company.

A 60-year Australian development stalwart, Meriton has built more than 80,000 apartments. Its current Cypress Palms project in Surfers Paradise includes a 90-storey tower while three-bedroom apartments start at $1.505 million.
Mr Tate awarded keys to the city in 2024 to Meriton's legendary founder Harry Triguboff. The mayor and other councillors all voted for a Meriton project that year too.
Meriton founder Harry Triguboff (centre) received the keys to the city from Gold Coast mayor Tom Tate in November 2024. ( Supplied )
But the land seller in the 2025 transfer of the land-purchase option to Mr Tate's company indicated they were upset.
Mr Turner said they would have sought a higher price if they had known Mr Tate's company would end up buying.
"It was worth more to Tom Tate than anyone else in the world," Mr Turner told the ABC.
Mr Turner said while they could have tried rejecting the sale, it ultimately proceeded after receiving advice to just take the offer and about any potential sale dispute dragging out.
A separate spat has emerged though about a real estate commission, with Mr Evans saying he was still seeking it from the Turner family company.
A development company of Tom Tate’s proposed a 389-unit residential tower and 216-apartment hotel on the site more than a decade ago. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins/Dominic Cansdale )
Mr Evans said he believed Meriton had genuinely planned to acquire the land, spending an "awful lot of money doing their due diligence (before) they transferred the option".

After Mr Tate's company acquired the final land sliver in July last year, he and partner companies sold all four blocks as a site. A subsidiary of AW Holding Group, developer of the Gold Coast's Jewel residences, acquired that site for $33 million in November 2025.
Mr Tate's company and those partners had paid more than $7 million acquiring blocks since 2007, according to records.

The mayor's involvement resurfaced after the politician in May last year recused himself when a majority of council rejected a proposed concrete batching project, near Burleigh, owned by the Turner family.

The mayor said then a "third party" was eyeing his Surfers Paradise land and the adjoining block of "Peter Turner", and while he did not believe a conflict of interest existed he would recuse himself.

But this August, with the land acquisition finished, the mayor voted for adopting a new council-staff recommendation about the concrete project. Court documents show council has agreed to drop opposition, subject to conditions, so ending a planning appeal from the Turner family business.

The mayor declined to say why he decided to vote this time, citing the appeal. Asked about handling any future Meriton projects before council, his office said Mr Tate "observes all applicable conflict of interest disclosure requirements".
Meriton said any council deals were conducted "at arms-length and through the standard planning process".

items.title: Our inflation is homegrown in Canberra
paras: Milton Friedman said it plainly half a century ago. Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon. It happens when the quantity of money grows faster than the quantity of goods and services it has to buy. No amount of official modelling about supply chains, Ukraine or the weather alters that arithmetic. Australia has now had two bouts of inflation in five years. Each has a monetary cause, and each was made in Canberra.
Start with the first. In 2020, the Commonwealth and the states chose to shut down large parts of the private economy. Output fell by about 7 per cent in a single quarter, the largest fall on record.

Spending did the opposite. JobKeeper cost $88.8 billion and paid an average of 3.6 million people a month in its first six months. Total direct Covid support came to about $311 billion. The Commonwealth ran deficits of $85.3 billion, $134.2 billion and $32 billion over three years, a total of $251.5 billion.

The Morrison government did not pay for this with taxes. Nor, in the end, did it pay with genuine borrowing from savers. The Reserve Bank bought about $260 billion of Commonwealth bonds between March 2020 and February 2022, almost exactly the size of the deficits. It bought another $57 billion of state bonds. It lent the banks $188 billion at 0.1 per cent. The legal nicety was that the bank bought the bonds from investors rather than straight from Treasury. The economics were identical. The deficit was paid for with money created from nothing.

So Friedman’s two conditions were met at once. The supply of goods was cut by decree. The supply of money was expanded by decree. Households, locked at home, banked the windfall. When the doors reopened, they spent it. Annual inflation went from minus 0.3 per cent in mid-2020 to 7.8 per cent by the end of 2022, the highest in more than three decades.

The official explanation still blames global supply shocks. But every country faced those shocks. The countries that suffered the worst inflation were those that printed money most freely. Australia was among them. Josh Frydenberg and Philip Lowe deserve most of the credit for the 2022 price surge, and Vladimir Putin rather less.

The printing presses stopped in February 2022. Since then the Reserve Bank has bought no bonds. Its holdings have shrunk by more than $120 billion as bonds mature. Yet inflation is back at 4.3 per cent, higher than in America, Britain, France or New Zealand. Friedman would ask where the money is coming from. The answer is now the banks.

Broad money has grown by roughly a quarter since the Albanese government took office in mid-2022, or close to 6 per cent a year. Bank credit is now growing at 8.4 per cent a year, with business credit up 11.3 per cent. When a bank writes a loan, it creates a deposit. The quantity theory does not care whether the money comes from the central bank or a commercial one.

Set that money growth against real output. Real GDP has grown at barely 2 per cent a year, and output per head is still lower than in June 2022. Money growing at close to 6 per cent, chasing output growing at barely 2, leaves roughly 4 per cent to be absorbed by prices. That is almost exactly the inflation rate we have. Friedman’s arithmetic works. The Treasurer’s excuses do not.

Government has not stood aside from this credit boom. It has fed it. Labor expanded its home guarantee scheme so that any first home buyer can borrow with a five-per-cent deposit, with Canberra standing behind the loan. Every such loan creates new money and new demand for a fixed stock of houses. Policy is pushing credit out of the banks while the Reserve Bank tries to rein it in.

Meanwhile the fiscal side has been funded the old-fashioned way, by tax and borrowing. Commonwealth payments rose from $616 billion in 2021-22 to $787 billion in 2025-26. Receipts rose by $180 billion over the same period, swollen by bracket creep that no parliament voted for. Gross debt rose by $76 billion. The states, led by Victoria, are borrowing heavily too. None of this is money printing. But it pulls labour and resources out of the private economy and into the public one.

The scale is extraordinary. Public spending has reached a record 28 per cent of GDP. The non-market sector of health, disability care, education and public administration produced 93 per cent of jobs growth in the year to late-2025. NDIS payments to participants were growing at 16 per cent a year.

And the productivity of that expanding sector is collapsing. Productivity in the non-market sector fell 6 per cent in the three years to 2024-25, the largest decline on record. Productivity across the whole economy has not grown in six years. Canberra is moving workers from activities where output per hour rises to ones where it falls. That shrinks the real output on which all the extra money must be spent. It is the denominator in Friedman’s equation, and the government is squeezing it.

So the two bouts of inflation share a single logic, but they differ in their mechanics. Under Morrison the numerator exploded. The Reserve Bank printed money to cover deficits while governments closed the private economy. Under Albanese the numerator keeps growing through bank credit, encouraged by government guarantees, while the denominator stalls. An ever larger, ever less productive public sector absorbs the labour that private firms need to grow.

The remedy follows directly. The Reserve Bank must never again finance a government deficit, through the front door or the back. Canberra should stop underwriting mortgage lending that inflates both credit and house prices. Spending growth, above all in the NDIS, must be brought back below the growth of the economy that pays for it. Tax brackets should be indexed so that inflation stops rewarding the Treasury. Above all, the private economy must be allowed to produce more.

Friedman also warned that inflation is a disease that can destroy a society. Australians have now caught it twice in five years. The first dose came from the printing press. The second comes from the banks and the bureaucracy. Both came from Canberra.
Peter Swan AO is Emeritus Professor of Finance at the UNSW-Sydney Business School

items.title: A tale of two economic models
paras: Every so often, politics runs an experiment that no economist could ever design. Take one people. Give them the same language, same history, same food, same customs, same climate, and the same stretch of earth. Then draw a line through the middle, hand each half a different operating system and watch what unfolds.

This experiment was run twice in the twentieth century, in Germany and in Korea. Both times the starting point was poverty. Both times one half became rich and the other stayed poor. The result was so lopsided that it ought to have ended the argument for good. Yet the argument keeps returning, wearing new clothes, using new words and promising a better ending.

Begin with Germany. In 1945, the country lay in ruins on both sides of what would become the inner German border. The people of Leipzig and Dresden were no less educated, no less industrious and no less German than the people of Hamburg and Munich. Saxony had been one of the great industrial heartlands of Europe. Nothing about the talent of the people explains what came next. Only the operating system does.

West Germany chose private property, open markets, a sound currency, and the rule of law. In 1948, price controls were swept away almost overnight, and shops that had been empty for years filled with goods within weeks. An economic miracle followed.
East Germany chose central planning, collectivisation and a state that decided what would be made, what it would cost and who would be allowed to have it.

East German families often waited more than a decade for a Trabant, a small two-stroke car with a plastic composite body. Housing was allocated, not chosen. Shelves held whatever the plan had decreed, which was rarely what anyone wanted. And a state that promised equality and called itself a workers’ paradise had to build a wall, guarded by guns and landmines, and recruit an army of informers to stop its people leaving utopia.

When the Berlin Wall came down in 1989, the truth spilled out. Factories were decades out of date. Rivers and air were badly polluted. The output figures the regime had boasted about for years were fiction.
Korea is a starker experiment because the socialist half began with the advantage. There the experiment continues to this day.

When the Korean Peninsula was divided in 1945, most of the heavy industry, hydroelectric dams and mines built under Japanese colonial rule lay in the north. The south was largely agricultural and desperately poor. At partition, the North was the richer half per head. That lead did not last.

Pyongyang in the North followed the planning playbook to the letter: land collectivisation, state ownership of everything worth owning, a cult of the leader and an economy run from the top. Seoul in the South, for all its early flaws and its own spells of authoritarian rule, bet on exports, private enterprise, and integration with the world economy.
By the 1970s, the South had overtaken the North, and the gap has widened ever since.

Today the Bank of Korea estimates that income per person in the North is roughly one twenty-eighth of that in the South. South Korea builds the mobile phones in our pockets, the ships in our harbours and the cars in our driveways. North Korea suffered a famine in the 1990s that killed hundreds of thousands of its own people.
Look at a satellite photograph of the Korean peninsula at night and you will see the South blazing with light and the North almost entirely dark.
Socialism did deliver equality, of a kind, in both those socialist countries: equality of poverty and equality of misery. But not for everyone.

The East German Politburo lived in a guarded compound where a special store stocked Western goods that ordinary citizens could only dream of. In Pyongyang, the ruling family and a loyal elite enjoy imported luxuries, private resorts, and the best of everything, while the countryside goes hungry.
Every regime that promises to abolish the privileged class simply installs a new one, smaller, harsher, and accountable to nobody.

When the state controls the economy, power over the economy becomes the only power that matters, and those who hold it look after themselves first. Concentrating every decision in the hands of planners does not abolish greed. It merely removes every check on it.
Australia is not about to become East Germany or North Korea. But the direction of travel matters.

Commonwealth payments are forecast at around 27 per cent of GDP this financial year, and gross debt is now more than $1 trillion. Industry policy increasingly means Canberra is choosing which sectors deserve taxpayer backing.

Taxes are rising, regulations multiplying, inflation persists, productivity languishes, and each new problem, including those government itself created, is met with the same reflex for more government.

The people who champion this path are mostly well-meaning. They sincerely believe that a little more planning, a little more redistribution, and a little more state direction will finally produce the fair and prosperous society that markets supposedly cannot. That is exactly what the planners in East Berlin and Pyongyang believed too.
But Australia is setting up a different experiment. What happens when a rich country adopts, piece by piece, the policies that kept poor countries poor.

The result will be worse, not better. A poor country has little left to lose. A rich one has a great deal, and its wealth rests on capital, skills and investment that can leave far faster than they arrived.

It has been seen before. Argentina was among the richest countries on earth a century ago, and Venezuela the richest in South America within living memory. Both have spent decades showing how much a rich country can lose and how quickly.

The lesson of Germany and Korea is not that every tax rise leads to a gulag. It is that prosperity is not a fixed pie waiting to be sliced more fairly by wise officials. It comes from free people: free to trade, free to keep what they earn, and free to fail.
Strip these things away, slowly, or quickly, and the pie shrinks for everyone except those holding the knife.
Anyone who believes that Australia’s current policy pathway leads to utopia should spend an afternoon looking at the evidence.
One half got Mercedes and Samsung. The other got the Trabant and a famine.

items.title: RBI Bulletin – November 2026
paras: Today, the Reserve Bank released the November 2026 issue of its monthly Bulletin. The Bulletin includes six speeches, four articles and current statistics. The four articles are: I. State of the Economy; II. Shifting Drivers of Imported Inflation: COVID-19 Pandemic to the West Asia Conflict; III. Performance of the NBFC Sector during 2025-26: A Review; and IV. Disentangling the Impact of US Monetary Policy on Indian Financial Markets: An Event Study Approach. I. State of the Economy Supply side challenges, elevated energy prices, and geopolitical uncertainty remain significant headwinds to the global economic outlook. Persistent inflationary pressures have led to synchronised monetary policy tightening across major central banks in the last three months. Pullback in AI-related stocks and elevated sovereign bond yields, despite some softening from multi-decade highs, remain a source of volatility in financial markets. Amidst uneven economic performance globally, the Indian economy stood out. High-frequency indicators of domestic economic activity showed resilience in October, underpinned by strong credit demand. Headline CPI inflation inched up, primarily driven by higher food inflation. With strong exports performance, the trade deficit narrowed in October as compared to corresponding month of the previous year. Equity markets rebounded supported by robust corporate earnings and foreign portfolio inflows. Net inflows under ECB and NRI deposits also remained strong. II. Shifting Drivers of Imported Inflation: COVID-19 Pandemic to the West Asia Conflict By Snehal S. Herwadkar, Ishu Thakur, Abhiruchi Rathi, Paras and Parul Arora This article examines how successive global shocks have reshaped the drivers of imported inflation in India. It constructs an import-intensity-weighted consumer price index (CPI) using item-level production, imports and exports data to assess the contribution of imported items to retail inflation. The analysis finds that food and fuel were the principal channels through which imported inflation impacted retail inflation during the COVID-19 pandemic as also during the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Precious metals became a key source of imported core inflation from 2025, while the West Asia conflict renewed crude oil-related pressures in 2026. Highlights: The import-intensity-weighted measure indicates that imported items account for 8.5 per cent of the new CPI basket (base 2024=100). Import intensity is highest for fuel and light, followed by food and beverages, and core components. Despite the small weight of imported items in CPI basket, it contributed around 18 per cent to the CPI headline inflation in October 2026. The West Asia conflict generated a sharper crude oil price shock than the Russia-Ukraine conflict. However, the pass-through to retail fuel prices in the current episode has been relatively lower, limiting the pressures on imported inflation. Higher precious metals prices emerged as another source of imported inflation since 2024. III. Performance of the NBFC Sector during 2025-26: A Review By Monalisa Poali, Pallavi Pant, Abhyuday Harsh and Brijesh P This article assesses the performance of the non-banking financial company (NBFC) sector as at end-March 2026. Highlights: The NBFC sector continued to demonstrate double-digit y-o-y credit growth along with improvement in asset quality at end-March 2026. Industry and retail segment accounted for the largest component of NBFCs’ loan portfolio. Within retail loans, vehicle, gold and microfinance loans accounted for the largest share. Higher growth in retail loans at end-March 2026 is driven by rapid growth in advances to individuals against gold. IV. Disentangling the Impact of US Monetary Policy on Indian Financial Markets: An Event Study Approach By Mayank Gupta, Anishma Sebastian, Bhanu Pratap and Thangzason Sonna This article examines how information conveyed by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announcements is associated with Indian financial markets. It distinguishes between monetary news, which signals tighter US monetary conditions, and growth news, which reflects stronger US economic prospects. It also examines these associations across conventional and unconventional US monetary policy phases. Highlights: Increase in US G-sec yields driven by monetary news are associated with rupee depreciation, higher Indian 10-year government bond yields and lower Sensex returns. Growth news shows no statistically significant association with the Indian financial variables. The exchange rate and government bond yield are significantly associated with monetary news during both conventional and unconventional US monetary policy phases. Sensex returns are significantly associated with monetary news during the conventional phase. India VIX shows no statistically significant association with either monetary or growth news. The main findings remain broadly consistent across alternative model specifications and news-classification thresholds. The views expressed in the Bulletin articles are those of the authors and do not represent the views of the Reserve Bank of India. (Brij Raj) Chief General Manager Press Release: 2026-2027/1563

items.title: ED arrests six persons in cross-border drugs smuggling network
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): The Enforcement Directorate ( ED ) has arrested six persons in connection with an investigation under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA) case linked to a cross-border drug smuggling network, the agency said on Tuesday. ED 's Delhi unit arrested these accused in different operations launched on October 11, October 18 and October 20. The arrested accused are identified as Lovejit Singh alias Labba, Manjeet Singh alias Manna, Prabhjit Singh, Gurjot Singh, Ramandeep Singh, and Gurpreet Singh. "A major drug trafficking operation involving smuggling of heroin from Afghanistan into India was unearthed during investigation," said the ED in a statement. The PMLA investigation was initiated on the basis of seizure of 293.81 kg of heroin from containers imported by Sandhu Exports at Nhava Sheva Port by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence and seizure of 352.71 kg of heroin from two vehicles and a flat in Faridabad, Haryana, by the Delhi Police Special Cell. Thus, a total of 646.52 kg of heroin has been seized so far. ED investigation revealed that the arrested persons, Lovejit Singh, Manjeet Singh, Ramandeep Singh, Gurjot Singh, Gurpreet Singh and Prabhjit Singh, coordinated the smuggling, storage and distribution of heroin across Punjab, Haryana, and Delhi.

"These individuals were key members of a syndicate that smuggled heroin from Afghanistan and Iran, concealing them within shipments of talc stone and gypsum powder," said the ED . Accused persons incorporated Sandhu Exports, a front company owned by Prabhjit Singh, to carry out the smuggling of drugs, informed the federal agency. ED uncovered the highly sophisticated heroin smuggling and money laundering network where identification of multiple bank accounts, cash transactions, and operational expenses by the accused has been made. "Accused disguised the origin of the illicit funds, which were further layered and integrated into seemingly legitimate financial activities. It was also revealed that the syndicate did not make any payments to Afghan suppliers until the drugs were sold in local markets." Further, the agency said the accused used cash payments to purchase multiple vehicles including Toyota Fortuner, Etios and Hyundai Verna etc in second hand market for trafficking from the storage Hubs to further distribution. The ED investigation revealed that cash was used for the purchase of high-end smartphones and encrypted communication apps were used to coordinate smuggling activities. "Drugs smuggled from Iran and Afghanistan used to be imported via the Nava Sheva port in Mumbai, later stored at a rented godown in Shivpuri, Madhya Pradesh and further distributed for local supply in parts of Delhi, Punjab and Haryana. Transportation was carried out in lesser quantities of 10 kg to prevent detection by law enforcement agencies. Earlier, a property in Jandoli Village (Rajpura, Punjab), multiple bank accounts in the names of accused persons, and fixed deposits have been attached by ED ," added the agency. (ANI)

items.title: Indian students in Kazan delighted as PM Modi arrives for BRICS Summit
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel Kazan [ Russia ], October 22 (ANI): Indian students in Kazan , Russia , are happy and excited about Prime Minister Narendra Modi's arrival at Hotel Korston , as he attends the 16th BRICS Summit . Notably, PM Narendra Modi on Tuesday touched down in Kazan city of Russia to participate in the 16th BRICS Summit and received a warm welcome. He is here to attend the 16th BRICS Summit , being held under the Chairmanship of Russia . To welcome PM Modi , students from India studying in Russia also sang a welcome song as they awaited PM Modi 's arrival at Hotel Korston . An Indian student from Pune, Saniya said that the students are quite excited to greet PM Modi . "Maybe we will get the opportunity (to meet PM Modi ) as many students are here (at Hotel Korston )... We are very excited. We are lucky to have this opportunity and we are happy to see him," she told ANI. An Indian student from Bihar, Shaurya Pratap said, "We are very happy to welcome PM Modi and we have prepared a song for him and we hope he likes it." Surbhi from Delhi said, "I have been here in Kazan since 2019 and today, we are going to sing a song for PM Modi and we are very excited about that." Parul, a final-year medical student, who has been in Kazan for the last five years told ANI, "We are really grateful that we got this opportunity to welcome our dear Prime Minister." Arti Pawar from Maharashtra said, "I have been living here for the past three years. I am very happy that PM Modi is coming here." Mrunmayi from Nagpur, Maharashtra said, "All the students here are quite enthusiastic as PM is going to come soon. We are too much delighted to welcome him." Meanwhile, ISKCON volunteers - from the Russia n and Indian communities were seen chanting 'Hare Krishna, Hare Ram' ahead of PM Modi 's arrival. While speaking with ANI, Sergoy, an ISKCON volunteer, said, "'Hare Krishna is a Mahamantra. This visit of PM Modi to Kazan , Russia is an important one for us. We are happy." Another ISKCON volunteer said, "We want to welcome PM Modi here in Kazan . It's a great honour for us to welcome him here We are very excited to see him." A Russia n citizen, Alexander said that the people there will welcome PM Modi by singing a song and that he is happy with PM Modi 's visit to Kazan . He said, "We have made a banner and we will also sing a song to welcome PM Modi ... I returned from India just two days back and directly came from Delhi to Kazan to see PM Modi . I am very happy that he is coming to Russia ." Notably, ahead of his departure to Russia , PM Modi shared a post on X and wrote, "Leaving for Kazan , Russia , to take part in the BRICS Summit . India attaches immense importance to BRICS, and I look forward to extensive discussions on a wide range of subjects. I also look forward to meeting various leaders there." The Prime Minister's office in a statement quoted PM Modi as saying, "I am departing today on a two-day visit to Kazan at the invitation of H.E. Mr. Vladimir Putin, President of the Russia n Federation, to attend the 16th BRICS Summit ." "India values the close cooperation within BRICS which has emerged as an important platform for dialogue and discussion on issues concerning the global developmental agenda, reformed multilateralism, climate change, economic cooperation, building resilient supply chains, promoting cultural and people to people connect, among others," PM Modi said. The statement further said that the expansion of BRICS with the addition of new members last year has added to its inclusivity and agenda for the global good. "Building upon the Annual Summit held in July 2024 in Moscow, my visit to Kazan will further reinforce the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between India and Russia . I look forward to meeting other leaders from BRICS as well," the PMO statement said. The 16th BRICS Summit in Kazan is being held under the chairmanship of Russia from October 22-24. During his visit, PM Modi is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with his counterparts from BRICS member countries and invited leaders in Kazan . The Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said, "The Summit, themed 'Strengthening Multilateralism for Just Global Development and Security,' will provide an important platform for leaders to discuss key global issues." It further said, "The Summit will offer a valuable opportunity to assess the progress of initiatives launched by BRICS and to identify potential areas for future collaboration." This visit marks, PM Modi 's second visit to Russia this year. He travelled to Moscow in July to attend the 22nd India- Russia Annual Summit where he held a bilateral meeting with President Putin. He was also conferred with Russia 's highest civilian award, the Order of St. Andrew the Apostle at the Kremlin in Moscow. BRIC, as a formal grouping, started after the meeting of the Leaders of Russia , India and China in St Petersburg on the margins of G8 Outreach Summit in 2006. The grouping was formalized during the first meeting of BRIC Foreign Ministers on the margins of UNGA in New York in 2006. The first BRIC Summit was held in Russia 's Yekaterinburg in 2009. It was agreed to expand BRIC into BRICS with the inclusion of South Africa at the BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting in New York in 2010. South Africa attended the 3rd BRICS Summit in Sanya in 2011. A further expansion of BRICS took place in 2024 with five new members - Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates. (ANI)

items.title: "Singapore plays key role in Act-East policy": Rajnath Singh at India-Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [ India ], October 22 (ANI): Dr. Ng Eng Hen , Singapore 's Minister of Defence , has begun his three-day visit to India . As part of his visit, Dr. Hen co-chaired the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi, with his India n counterpart Rajnath Singh . The Summit began on Tuesday morning, with India n Defence Minister Rajnath Singh welcoming the Singapore delegation warmly. He noted that the strategic partnership the two countries share is a "testimony of increasing closeness between our countries." Singh said, " The meeting is happening at a time when India marks the decade of India 's Act in Policy, in which Singapore has played a key role in promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and developed strategic connectivity with country institutions." Building upon Singh's remarks, Dr. Ng Eng Hen said, "You reminded us that this is the 10th year since your Act East Policy. From Singapore 's perspective, India has always been part of the East. Whether you choose to act or look, we consider you part of the area." He said that while remembering the history of Singapore , India has been an important partner. " When we started the Singapore armed forces, one of the countries that we asked early on to see whether they could help us was India ." Hen highlighted that such historical memoirs serve as important reminders and "reflects how we feel that India is very part of our area. We are delighted that our ten years of bilateral relations have been very much improved in defence and all-round strategic partnership." Hen also thanked PM Modi for visiting Singapore earlier this year and noted that the visit was an excellent meeting. A day before, the Ministry of Defence had announced the sixth India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue in New Delhi on October 22, 2024. The release noted that between India and Singapore , "The engagements have diversified to include wide-ranging contacts between the Services, military-to-military exchanges, high-level visits, capacity building and training programs, cooperation in UN Peacekeeping, ship visits and bilateral exercises." Inaugurated in 2016, the India - Singapore Defence Ministers' Dialogue is a key platform to strengthen bilateral defence cooperation between Singapore and India . The fifth edition of the Defence Ministers' Dialogue took place in January 2021 through virtual teleconference. During the meeting, the two parties showed confidence in the outcomes of the meeting that would result in providing impetus to the entire spectrum of the bilateral engagement as well as to the regional security architecture. (ANI)

items.title: "India matters most for future of planet" says British High Commissioner Lindy Cameron
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): In recent times when climate change has become a pressing issue with countries across the world being ravaged due to climate catastrophes, it becomes imperative to discuss and deliberate upon global actions that can help the world rise up and meet these challenges. At the NDTV World Summit's a discussion was held on the theme, "India Matters The Most For Future Of Planet". Participants in the discussion included Erik Solheim, Former Minister of Climate and the Environment of Norway; Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India; Shishir Priyadarshi, President Chintan Research Foundation; Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative. "India is the country that matters the most for the future of the planet and climate change. India's ambition for development should not in any way be constrained by the responsibilities of the planet," Lindy Cameron , British High Commissioner to India, emphasised. She noted that the UK is committed towards the Multilateral Development Banks (MDB) reforms, technology and research support in India to aid the efforts. "Every dollar invested in resilient infrastructure pays 4 times over," said Cameron. "Lived experience of climate emergencies helps people to understand why their government needs to take policy action now," she added. Further talking about the need for urgent government action, Harjeet Singh, Global Engagement Director, Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said, "Series of disasters affecting both developed and developing countries are serving as a wake-up call. As rich countries will get more and more affected by climate change which they did not imagine till a couple of years ago, most vulnerable countries are going to be struggling with impacts who also have very less capacity to deal with it. India is taking a leadership role in the global fight against climate change. Initiatives such as Global Biofuels Alliance, International Solar Alliance, and Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure are some efforts taken by India in recent years to manage the climate crisis. (ANI)

items.title: Asia's Largest Mindfulness India Summit 2024 Marks a New Era for Corporate Culture and Personal Well-being with the Inau
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel PNN Mumbai (Maharashtra) [India], October 22: The Mindfulness India Summit 2024, an initiative by the Mindful Science Centre, presented by HSBC and supported by CII Leadership and HR Committee, successfully concluded its two-day event on October 17 and 18, 2024, establishing new benchmarks in corporate culture and personal well-being. With over 40 international and national experts addressing mindfulness, emotional intelligence, and neuroscience, the summit highlighted how these principles are essential in transforming leadership, enhancing employee engagement, and fostering sustainable well-being within organizations. The evolving workplace landscape, particularly the increasing role of AI, requires a renewed focus on human-centric leadership and emotional resilience. The summit provided a platform for forward-thinking leaders to explore how mindfulness can effectively bridge this gap, ensuring both corporate excellence and employee well-being . The summit featured MasterChef Sanjeev Kapoor as the Chief Guest, who shared how mindful leadership has played a pivotal role in building his culinary empire. Along with Chris Ruane, Ex MP British Parliament and Chair of Mindfulness Initiative UK, J N Behl and Global Holistic Health Guru Mickey Mehta, Kapoor also launched Manish Behl's new book "Observe - 101 Mindfulness Practices", a guide designed to make mindfulness accessible for both professionals and individuals in their everyday lives. Behl, a global mindfulness expert and founder of the Mindful Science Centre, shared, "With this book, I want to demystify mindfulness and make it accessible to everyone. Mindfulness is not a complex or distant concept, but a practical tool for reducing stress, improving focus, and fostering deeper connections in both personal and professional settings." The Mindfulness India Summit 2024 has successfully proven that mindfulness is no longer a luxury but a necessity in modern corporate structures. By adopting mindfulness practices, organizations are not only creating more compassionate work environments but are also enhancing their overall performance and sustainability in a world increasingly shaped by technological and emotional complexity. The 2 days also saw the launch of Mindfulness Impact Awards, to honor organizations and individuals who have integrated mindfulness into their corporate structures and personal lives. These awards reflect the growing recognition that workplace culture directly affects employee productivity, creativity, and overall well-being. Manish Behl, founder of the awards, explained, "Corporate success today goes beyond profit; it's about fostering environments where employees thrive mentally, emotionally, and physically. Our vision with these awards is to inspire a deeper integration of mindfulness in corporate cultures worldwide. By recognizing these pioneers, we hope these awards inspire companies and individuals to further integrate mindfulness into their environments, ultimately fostering happier, more productive workplaces, communities, and a more compassionate world." The awards were designed to acknowledge champions of mindfulness across categories, recognizing those who incorporate mindful practices to improve workplace culture, employee engagement, and societal impact. Winners ranged from corporate giants like Aditya Birla Group and Accenture to global educators and community leaders. Award Winners Include: - Entrepreneur: Mickey Mehta (India) - Commitment: Aditya Birla Group, Accenture (India) - Champions: IPG Mediabrands (India) - Communities: HPCL (India) - Champions: Hincolas (India)

items.title: "No shortage of oil in world and prices should hopefully come down", says Hardeep Singh Puri
paras: Join our Whatsapp channel New Delhi [India], October 22 (ANI): Hardeep Singh Puri, Minister for Petroleum and Natural Gas on Tuesday said that there is no shortage of oil in the world and prices will come down soon, answering the question of the recent upswing in crude oil prices. Speaking to the media, the Union Minister cited global factors such as the war in the Middle East and voluntary cuts in oil production which are influencing the oil prices in the global market. He said, "It depends on global factors. One thing is very clear, there is no shortage of oil in the world...Today, more and more oil is coming on the market...There are other factors like geopolitical tensions. So, there is no shortage of oil but if there is tension in one part of the world, then the freight cost, and insurance freight cost will go up. Today, let us all hope that better sense prevails, that call for peace that our Prime Minister has been making from every forum...There is more than enough oil in the world and prices should hopefully come down. That's my expectation..." "If there's tension in one part of the world, then the cost of, if you have to take a longer route, then the cost of the freight cost, the insurance rate cost, that will go up...There's more than enough oil in the world, and prices should hopefully come down," he commented in his personal capacity.

The union minister said many countries such as Brazil, and Guayana among others are coming with their oil. Citing the stable prices in the last 3 years, the minister said that the government is taking every possible step to ensure stable oil prices. "Central government at every stage has stepped in to cushion and bring the prices down from November 2021 to May 2022. Now there are some global factors. The cost at the retail point is determined by the cost of the barrel in the international market plus the cost of transportation, freight, insurance, retailers, refining cost and margin, then dealers, margin, etc. We are solving all the problems we can, now you tell the global community to hold and bring them down," he added. This comes after oil prices rose nearly 2 per cent on Monday, reclaiming major losses from last week's sell-off. Brent crude features upped by $1.44, or 1.97 per cent in the afternoon. Earlier this month, Puri had said that the country is well-prepared to meet its growing energy demands, with a diverse range of oil sources. Speaking on the availability of oil in the global market, Puri emphasised that India has expanded its procurement base, moving from 27 suppliers to 39. (ANI)

items.title: Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets
paras: Decades-long conspiracy Guilty: Huawei faces steep penalties for stealing T-Mobile, Cisco trade secrets Huawei didn’t try very hard to hide thefts of US trade secrets, DOJ says.

31 ... ... ... Credit: Feature China / Contributor | Future Publishing Credit: Feature China / Contributor | Future Publishing Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav On Tuesday, a US jury convicted one of China’s key telecommunications and AI giants, Huawei Technologies, of stealing trade secrets from US tech firms and evading sanctions against Iran.

Although the longrunning charges stem back to 2018, the verdict coming now threatens to inflame US-China tensions at a sensitive time, just as Donald Trump prepares to increase tariffs on China . In a press release , however, the US Department of Justice celebrated the outcome as critical to protecting the US financial system, the global telecommunications industry, and US national security.
The jury convicted Huawei of charges including bank fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US, money laundering conspiracy, and “substantive” violations of the International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Among crimes, Huawei was found guilty of “repeatedly” lying to banks about its business in Iran. Huawei also frequently lied to the US government that “it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said. In reality, the DOJ proved at trial that Huawei was conducting business in Iran under the name “Skycom” to evade sanctions, while providing Iran with “turnkey services with respect to an Internet backbone and broader accessibility for mobile networks.” Further, Huawei helped the Iranian regime “monitor and censor its users’ access to the Internet” and provided surveillance cameras to monitor protests, the DOJ said. In a statement, the acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, M. Scott Proctor, said Huawei “empowered our enemies” and “harmed our national security.”

As the DOJ successfully argued, Huawei lied about its Iranian business specifically so that it could continue obtaining billions in US dollars by participating in a global marketplace that gave it necessary access to steal US tech. Among companies targeted, US Attorney for the Eastern District of New York Joseph Nocella Jr. said that Huawei blatantly stole from T-Mobile and Cisco, as well as a semiconductor storage company called CNEX and an antenna manufacturer called Quintel.

“The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for Internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology,” the DOJ said.

T-Mobile’s “Tappy” targeted by Huawei. via DOJ DOJ shared evidence of Huawei technology theft. via DOJ DOJ shared evidence of Huawei technology theft. via DOJ T-Mobile’s “Tappy” targeted by Huawei. via DOJ DOJ shared evidence of Huawei technology theft. via DOJ One of the stolen ideas was the design of a T-Mobile robot called “Tappy,” which helped the US firm “assess the responsiveness of touch screens by mimicking a human touch,” the DOJ said. To copy the design, Huawei signed a non-disclosure agreement, then sent photos and technical details back to China. Even bolder, when that intel was deemed insufficient, “a Huawei employee stole a part of the robot in his backpack and carried it out of T-Mobile’s controlled laboratory,” the DOJ said.

Huawei’s tactics weren’t always sophisticated, but they were effective, the DOJ said, building into “a long-running conspiracy to steal intellectual property of US companies.” At trade shows and tours of rivals’ facilities, Huawei employees would pretend to “get lost,” the DOJ said, so they could wander into restricted areas and take photos of hardware, The New York Times reported .

Huawei engineers would also sometimes hide their activity by spelling words backwards. For example, Huawei was able to copy the source code used on Cisco routers—which the DOJ said was “identified as the ‘crown jewel’ of Cisco technology”—by taking notes in which they spelled Cisco as “ocsic.” Another time, the DOJ noted that a Huawei employee was caught “photographing proprietary Fujitsu equipment” while wearing a badge that falsely identified him as an employee of “Weihua.”

During the trial, Meredith Arfa, a federal prosecutor, noted that Huawei employees were sometimes paid bonuses for their crimes, since the theft was so integral to Huawei’s business model, NYT reported.

Roman Rozhavsky, the assistant director of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said that Huawei spent years expanding its international enterprise “through theft of trade secrets, fraud, and other criminal conduct at the expense of US companies and the rule of law.”

Huawei has been banned from selling its tech in the US since 2019, so NYT noted that the guilty verdict is unlikely to rattle the company’s finances much. However, the financial penalties stemming from the verdict could be steep, as the DOJ explained that they include “criminal fines, forfeiture, and restitution.”

Huawei continues to deny any wrongdoing and rejects US claims that the Chinese Communist Party directed the thefts. NYT noted that Huawei’s investors have argued that the US fight is politically motivated and seeks to hobble “a Chinese initiative to build 5G networks around the world.”

Outside the courthouse following the verdict, Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, told reporters that it’s significant that the jury did not convict Huawei of racketeering charges or conspiracy to obstruct justice. According to Heberlig, the examples of US technology theft merely represented “isolated misconduct by company employees,” which inevitably happens in a company so large, with “hundreds of thousands of people.”
Heberlig confirmed that Huawei planned to appeal and considered the jury’s opposition to racketeering charges to be a “profound rejection of the United States’ narratives about what Huawei is.”

“The allegations that the government made in this case overreached and simply weren’t consistent with the successful, innovative and hard-working company that we came to know and deeply respect in this trial,” Heberlig said.
After the verdict, China “lashed out” at the US, AFP reported . According to Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun, the US is trying to use the ruling to “suppress” Huawei.
China “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests,” Guo said.
However, the FBI’s Rozhavsky suggested that even China, which frequently negotiates with Trump as the trade rivals continually clash, can’t spare Huawei from substantial penalties.

“This case serves as a stark reminder that the Chinese government continues to pose a serious threat to our economic and national security, but today’s guilty verdict proves the FBI and our partners will aggressively investigate, expose, and hold accountable those who target our nation,” Rozhavsky said. “No company is too big, too powerful, or too well connected to exploit the US and its citizens and expect to escape American justice.”

items.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
paras: Paying for Email? Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.

0 ... ... ... This dog is Kagi's mascot; you'll see it on the search engine homepage, too. Credit: Kagi This dog is Kagi's mascot; you'll see it on the search engine homepage, too. Credit: Kagi Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.
If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.
That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

According to the company, Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers. Compared to the number of people using Google Search or even Bing or DuckDuckGo, that’s not much. But the pitch is that with Google, the user is the product, not the customer, and that paying anywhere from $5 to $25 per month (there are multiple plans; unlimited search queries is in the $10 per month plan) helps users escape from that devil’s bargain.

Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.

The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative, more sensible, and optional.

Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.

Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

items.title: Seabird ‘spies’ could help spot ships that aren’t broadcasting their location
paras: Facebook Threads X / Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn Reddit Email Print A northern gannet ( Morus bassanus ) tagged with biologging devices on its back and tail Steve Votier Audio from seabirds fitted with mini recording devices and GPS trackers has been used by researchers to show that marine life can record encounters with vessels that are otherwise difficult to track.

Many large vessels are now legally required to carry automatic identification systems broadcasting their identity and location at regular intervals. Although this has allowed interactions between animals and fisheries to be studied at scale, there are enormous gaps in coverage.

In fact, recent research suggests that three-quarters of industrial fishing vessels don’t use the technology, says Jonathan Rutter at the University of Oxford. This is partly because regulations on the types of vessels that are required to share data vary by country. Large satellite ‘blind spots’ also contribute to the problem, he says, and so does subterfuge for the purpose of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing (IUU).

Rutter says that being caught as bycatch in fishing is one of the greatest risks to seabird populations, but if fishing vessels are only tracked “with conventional methods, such footprints of risk may be strikingly incomplete”.

The team analysed audio collected from devices attached to seven northern gannets ( Morus bassanus ) and found that one third of the audio detections couldn’t be matched with vessel tracking data – mostly off the UK coast.

Overall, 12 per cent of the vessel detections made by the four critically endangered Balearic shearwaters ( Puffinus mauretanicus ) included in the study couldn’t be matched to public data. But given the high vessel density where they were – off the Catalan coast – the researchers estimated that up to 20 per cent of the vessels detected by the four birds weren’t broadcasting their identity.

Tammy Davies at BirdLife International – a global partnership of non-governmental organisations – who wasn’t involved in the study, says the research could “give us a more complete picture of the risks seabirds face at sea” and “ultimately, this could contribute to better assessments of bycatch risk and help identify fisheries and areas where conservation measures are most needed”.
Peter Ejbye-Ernst at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement (NSCR), describes the study as “fascinating” from a green criminology point of view, too.
“What this study is somewhat proposing is that we can also look outside of humans for witnesses too,” he says, which overcomes a key barrier in observing crime at sea.
In terms of its applications for cracking down on IUU, he says: “There’s a fine line between trying to understand something better and document it and then trying to control it and surveil it.”

There are caveats, as the study has a small sample size and records both false-negatives and false-positives. It also gives very little information on the type of activity vessels were carrying out. But, while the research isn’t a solution to the problem of IUU, it is “part of the toolbox” for understanding what is happening at sea, says Ejbye-Ernst.
The study didn’t differentiate between the size of vessels, but Rutter and his colleagues say this would be a good area for future research.
Photographer Nicole Tung captures the tough world facing South-East Asia’s fishers and their families in this series of images, which won her the Carmignac Photojournalism Award for fieldwork

“Animal-borne audio recorders could potentially be used to investigate other ecological interactions and human activities that are difficult to observe directly, particularly in the marine environment,” says team member Ana Bertoldi Carneiro , also at BirdLife International.

Hugo Tagholm at the charity Oceana says it is shocking that so many of the interactions were with unseen vessels, but he is concerned about attaching devices to seabirds on a broader scale to track this.
“Seabirds are already grappling with the harm caused by overfishing and climate breakdown, we don’t want to put them at even greater risk from vessel operators acting illegally,” he says.

“What we need is mandatory remote electronic monitoring across all fishing vessels, clear and effective laws and catch limits to protect and restore our seas, and truly deterrent sanctions for those breaking the law.”

items.title: Kwon stuns Cobolli, Italy and Korea level at 1-1: the doubles will decide
paras: In Bologna, Lorenzo Musetti gave the three-time defending champions the lead against Hong Seong-chan before Kwon Soon-woo beat Flavio Cobolli in a final-set tie-break. The doubles will decide who faces Czechia in the semi-finals.

Kwon Soon-woo kept South Korea alive in its first Davis Cup Final 8. 156 beat Flavio Cobolli 3-6, 7-6 (3), 7-6 (5) in 2 hours 50 minutes on Wednesday in Bologna to level the quarter-final against Italy at 1-1, after Lorenzo Musetti beat Hong Seong-chan 6-0, 7-6 (5).

The doubles will decide who faces Czechia in the semi-finals. Kwon went straight back on court for the doubles with Chung Hyeon against Matteo Berrettini and Andrea Vavassori, with only 20 minutes to recover. “I mean, Captain wants, but I will talk to Captain now,” he said after his win, looking at Korea captain Chung Jong-sam.

items.title: “I think I am innocent”: Zverev stands by his L’Équipe words, “not too concerned” by Patea case

items.title: How Alexander Zverev’s 2026 season compares to Andy Murray’s when he became world number one
paras: The German star began the year ranked third – behind Carlos Alcaraz and Jannik Sinner – and had yet to win a Grand Slam title. The narrative around Zverev has completely shifted within 11 months, as he has now won two major titles and achieved the world number one ranking for the first time in his career .

Around 10 years ago, Andy Murray also disrupted the dominance of multiple juggernauts, rising above Novak Djokovic, Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer to achieve the number one ranking. As already mentioned, Zverev captured his first Grand Slam titles this year, winning Roland Garros and the US Open.

How would you rate the 2026 WTA and ATP seasons out of 10? Elena Rybakina and Alexander Zverev are your year-end number ones… The 30-year-old defeated Flavio Cobolli in the Parisian final, and overcame the challenge presented by home favourite Ben Shelton in the New York-based championship match.

Friendships are built by repeated contact, not by being liked
items.hook: This is the single most useful fact in the whole guide.
paras: Studies of primary-school classrooms found that children seated next to each other were far more likely to become friends than children seated across the room. When teachers changed the seating, new friendships formed with the new neighbours.

So the engine is: same place, same people, same activity, over and over. The day at the yo-yo bar followed by basketball is that engine working - shared activity changed how the other boy treated him. It was not luck.
items.do: Pick one activity he already likes and commit to it weekly for a full term.

items.title: Keep the proximity - change the watching
items.hook: Your instinct is half right, and the other half matters.
paras: You are right that being around the group matters: children nominate as friends the children they see and interact with most. 'Out of sight, out of mind' is real for acquaintances.

But guidance written for schools is blunt: merely remaining beside a group is not friendship. A child who hovers is read as a bystander rather than a player, and it holds him in the one-down position. Watching has a use - but only as the first twenty seconds of joining in, never as the endpoint.
items.do: Keep telling him to stay near the group. Add: 'then take a job in the game'.

items.title: Teach 'watch, then blend'
items.hook: The best way to join a game is not to ask.
paras: Most of us were told to walk up and say 'Can I play?' But that makes everyone stop and look at him, and makes 'no' very easy.

The better sequence, used by people who study play: watch for about twenty seconds to learn the game and where the line is, then slide into the action without stopping it. Take the end of the line. Stand in the outfield. Pick up the ball and pass it back.
items.do: Rehearse it at home in five minutes. Ask him to name the 'easiest job' in each game.

items.title: Host one friend at a time - this is the biggest lever you control
items.hook: The child who invites is rarely short of friends.
paras: Pick a child he has had fun with in the last month, not someone he admires from afar. Invite one person for one to two hours. Put away anything precious, have two activities ready, start with a snack, and let the guest choose sometimes.
Keep it short and end while they are both still enjoying it. Then leave a few weeks before inviting the same child again, so the invitation can come back to him.
items.do: Text one parent this week and set a date for the school holidays.

items.title: Ask the teacher one specific question
items.hook: Teachers see the playground. Ask them to name names.
paras: Ask two things: who does he play well with, and could he be seated near them or paired with them for group work?
Seating is one of the few levers that reliably creates new friendships, and it is invisible to the children - no one has to know it was arranged.
items.do: Email the teacher this week with those two questions.

items.title: Do not push into a group that is rejecting him
items.hook: Here the advice is the opposite of persistence.
paras: Where a group is actively excluding him, the guidance is to back off - when you back off from people, they can move towards you. Put his energy into two or three other children instead of one closed circle.
Friends in more than one place - school, a club, family friends - also make him far less vulnerable when one group turns cold.
items.do: Help him list three children outside the difficult group he could get to know.

items.title: One or two good friends is the goal - not popularity
paras: Kids need one or two good friends. You do not need to worry about him being the most popular child in the class.
His warmth and kindness are already the raw material. Treat this as coaching a skill, not fixing a fault - if he feels like a project, he will resist.
items.do: Say his strengths out loud, often. Confidence is what carries a child into a group.

items.title: Playing and talking with girls is normal and good
items.hook: Children believe gender matters far more than it actually does.
paras: In one large classroom experiment, simply seating boys and girls next to each other doubled how often they became friends.
Girls' play tends to build conversation, turn-taking and inventing games together; boys' play builds bigger, faster group play. Being good at both widens his circle.
items.do: No action needed. Just do not let him think it is odd.

items.title: When to get more help
items.hook: Ordinary friendship difficulty is not a disorder.
paras: Get more support if he becomes reluctant to go to school, is persistently distressed, has changes in sleep or appetite, or says it is happening all the time and he cannot make it stop.
Start with his teacher, then the school counsellor, then your GP for a referral. Kids Helpline is free and open 24/7 on 1800 55 1800, for children and for parents.
items.do: Save Kids Helpline in your phone: 1800 55 1800.
